sections.title: Basic Concept of Mixtures and Alligation
sections.content: Mixture problems involve combining two or more substances to form a new mixture. Alligation is a quick calculation method used to determine the ratio in which two ingredients with different prices or percentages should be mixed. Step 1: Identify the price or percentage of both ingredients. Step 2: Identify the mean value (price/percentage of the mixture). Step 3: Use the alligation rule to find the mixing ratio.

sections.title: Basic Alligation Rule
sections.content: Step 1: Write the prices of the two ingredients (Cheap and Dear). Step 2: Write the mean price in the middle. Step 3: Take cross differences. Step 4: The resulting values give the mixing ratio. Example: Sugar priced at ₹40 and ₹60 is mixed to obtain a mean price of ₹50. Ratio = (60−50):(50−40) = 10:10 = 1:1.

sections.title: Milk and Water Profit Concept
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the cost price of milk. Step 2: If water is added for free, the cost of the mixture decreases. Step 3: Determine the quantity of water based on the desired profit percentage. Step 4: Convert the ratio to find the percentage of water. Example: If a 20% profit is required and the mixture is sold at the cost price of milk, approximately 20% water can be added.

sections.title: Single Replacement Method
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the total quantity of the mixture. Step 2: Remove 'x' liters of the mixture. Step 3: Add the same amount of a new ingredient. Step 4: Calculate the new composition of the mixture. Example: If 2 liters are removed from 10 liters of milk and replaced with water, the quantity of milk decreases.

sections.title: Concept of Repeated Replacement
sections.content: Step 1: In each step, a portion of the mixture is removed. Step 2: The same quantity of a new substance is added. Step 3: The amount of the original substance keeps decreasing at every step. Step 4: Observe the pattern and perform the calculation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Taking the cross difference incorrectly in alligation. 2. Writing the mean price in the wrong position. 3. Forgetting that water is considered free in milk-water problems. 4. Forgetting that the total quantity remains constant in replacement problems.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In mixture questions, the alligation rule is the fastest method. Cross difference gives the mixing ratio. In milk-water problems, water is considered free, which increases profit. In replacement problems, the total quantity remains constant but the composition changes.

tricks.title: Alligation Cross Trick
tricks.explanation: Write cheap and dear prices and perform cross subtraction.

tricks.title: Profit = Water Percentage Trick
tricks.explanation: If milk is sold at its cost price, the profit percentage is approximately equal to the percentage of water added.
tricks.example: For 20% profit, approximately 20% water can be added.

tricks.title: Cheap Ingredient Will Be More
tricks.explanation: The mean price always lies between the two prices, so the cheaper ingredient will be in greater quantity.
tricks.example: In a mixture of ₹40 and ₹60, the ₹40 ingredient will be in larger quantity.

tricks.title: Quick Ratio Method
tricks.explanation: The cross difference directly gives the final mixing ratio.

tricks.title: Replacement Logic
tricks.explanation: When mixture is removed and replaced with water, the original ingredient decreases.
tricks.example: From 10L mixture, removing 2L and adding water reduces the amount of milk.

tricks.title: Mean Value Identification
tricks.explanation: The mean value will always lie between the cheap and dear values.
tricks.example: For ₹30 and ₹70, a possible mean value is ₹50.

tricks.title: Percentage to Ratio Trick
tricks.explanation: Profit percentage can be directly converted into a ratio.

tricks.title: Quick Check Rule
tricks.explanation: The final mixture price will always lie between the original prices.
